🚗 Robotaxi Arrives With 'No Steering Wheel, No Pedals'; The Car Has Officially Removed The Two Things You Use To Disagree With It

AUSTIN — reported from the back seat, where all seats now are

WHEELS — A carmaker unveiled its long-teased purpose-built robotaxi, proudly noting it ships with no steering wheel and no pedals — a bold design choice that trades every controls you might reach for in a panic for the serene confidence that the software has this, definitely, probably.

"Just get in and relax," the company said, of a vehicle that has thoughtfully eliminated your ability to do anything else. Riders in the invite-only launch described the experience as smooth, futuristic, and only occasionally accompanied by the primal instinct to grab a wheel that is no longer there. Analysts note it is the purest expression yet of the 2026 bargain: hand over the controls, and in exchange receive a very nice place to sit while you think about that decision.

🤝 Chip Giant Buys The Famous A.I. Model Hub; The Company That Sells The Shovels Now Owns The Front Door To The Mine

SILICON VALLEY — reported from a very expensive handshake

DEALS — The world's most valuable chipmaker announced it is acquiring the beloved open hub where developers share A.I. models — meaning the company that already sells nearly every shovel in the gold rush now also owns the counter where everyone picks up their maps.

"It's about community," the buyer said warmly, of a purchase that quietly completes a set. Observers note the strategy has a certain elegance: first sell the hardware everyone needs, then buy the town square where they gather to use it, and finally sit back as the entire industry politely files past your cash register on its way to build the future.

💰 Chip Firm Says The A.I. Money Just Keeps Coming; The Quarter's Real Winners Were The People Selling Picks To Everyone Digging

THE EARNINGS CALL — reported over the sound of applause it wanted more of

MARKETS — A major chip supplier raised its outlook for A.I. revenue into the tens of billions, confirming what everyone suspected: in a gold rush, the surest fortune belongs not to the miners but to the calm person at the trading post selling them each a pick, a pan, and a subscription.

"Demand remains extraordinary," the company said, of a business so good that a record-breaking beat somehow still disappointed a crowd that had priced in miracles. Analysts note the modern A.I. economy has a reliable shape: thousands of companies race to strike it rich, a handful of suppliers get rich selling them the equipment, and everyone agrees this is fine right up until someone asks who's actually finding gold.

📈 Cloud-Data Company Jumps 22% Because A.I. Now Helps Write The Code; The Software That Makes Software Made The Stock Go Up

WALL STREET — reported from a green arrow, briefly

STOCKS — A cloud-data firm's shares leapt after strong results it credited partly to A.I. coding tools speeding up how fast software gets built — a virtuous loop in which computers write the programs that make the company that sells computing that trains the computers that write the programs.

"Productivity is accelerating," executives said, of an era where the machines have started doing their own homework. Analysts welcomed the results while noting a faint philosophical vertigo: the industry has finally built software good enough to build more software, which is either the beginning of infinite progress or simply the fastest way yet devised to generate an even longer to-do list.

🔌 A.I. Data-Center Boom Meets A Deeply Human Problem: The Electric Bill; The Future Is Incredibly Bright, Please Don't Run The Microwave

THE POWER GRID — reported by dimming lights

ENERGY — As companies race to build ever-larger data centers to feed the A.I. boom, they keep running into a stubbornly old-fashioned obstacle — there is only so much electricity, and the machines of the future are extraordinarily thirsty for it.

"We're scaling capacity aggressively," operators said, of an industry that has discovered its dazzling digital dreams are ultimately powered by the same wall socket as your toaster. Experts note the irony is complete: humanity built a superintelligence to solve every hard problem, then immediately handed it the hardest one of all, which is finding enough outlets to keep itself turned on.
